tagline: From Cleopatra Hill’s mining town to the Verde Valley’s old downtowns
intro: This drive descends from Jerome toward the Verde Valley, then follows Historic 89A through the old downtowns of Clarkdale and Cottonwood. In Jerome, buildings line winding roads on the steep mountainside. The Arizona Department of Transportation designated the Jerome-Clarkdale-Cottonwood Historic Road in 1992; the historic route is about 10 miles long.

United Verde built wagon roads from Jerome to Prescott, the Verde Valley and the railway depot at Ash Fork. Expensive wagon transport and a sharp copper-price fall helped bring operations to a halt in 1884. The larger highway first entered the state system in 1927 as State Route 79, when only the Prescott-to-Clarkdale portion had been built. Pavement reached the Jerome-to-Cottonwood section before the entire highway was paved in 1938. The highway became U.S. 89A in 1941 and State Route 89A in 1993. The historic route now takes in the downtown streets while the state highway follows a different course through Clarkdale and Cottonwood.

Begin with Jerome on Cleopatra Hill, above the valley communities of Clarkdale and Cottonwood. From the roundabout at Clarkdale Parkway, the historic route runs north, then follows Main Street and Broadway through Clarkdale. It passes Tuzigoot National Monument before becoming Cottonwood’s Main Street and meeting Cottonwood Street.

moments.title: Jerome
moments.text: Jerome’s buildings follow winding streets across a steep mountainside, the setting of a copper town that outlived its mines. Mining ended in 1953, and the population fell below 100. Residents organized the Jerome Historical Society that year and opened a museum and gift shop as they turned to tourism. In 1956, the society completed negotiations with Phelps Dodge to prevent further demolition in the town’s main section. Formerly vacant buildings now house gift, antique and craft shops, and the former high school complex contains artists’ galleries. Society plaques identify historic properties among the surviving buildings.

moments.title: Clarkdale
moments.text: Clarkdale was planned around the work of processing Jerome’s copper ore. William A. Clark founded the company town in 1912, with services that included electricity, telephones, sewers and spring water. That planning also enforced divisions: engineers and executives lived in Upper Clarkdale, while workers occupied Lower Clarkdale. Mexican and Mexican-American laborers were restricted to Patio Town, with a separate pool and park. The mine and smelter closed in 1953. Clarkdale incorporated four years later, and a cement plant followed in 1959. The original town site is on the National Register, and the Clark Memorial Clubhouse and Memorial Library remain in use.

moments.title: Tuzigoot
moments.text: Tuzigoot’s 110 rooms occupy a ridge above the Verde River floodplain. The Sinagua built the pueblo above farmland, with the Verde River and Black Hills providing resources. Few doorways pierce the rooms; residents used ladders through roof openings. Excavation took place from 1933 to 1935, followed by work to prepare the ruins for public display. The National Park Service identifies a room rebuilt in the 1930s whose roof was not part of its original form. The museum displays artifacts found at the site, while Tavasci Marsh provides perennial wetlands nearby.
moments.notice: Look at the stone rooms extending along the ridge’s spine.
